gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a named reviewer's measured usable AC energy for any candidate. Every runtime table assumes 85%. The measured figures are: StorageReview got 1,910 Wh (92%) out of the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 at about 1 kW, StorageReview got 1,800 Wh (88%) out of the EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max at 350 W, Notebookcheck got 1,600 Wh (79%) out of the Anker SOLIX C2000 Gen 2 at 200 W, and OutdoorGearLab got 1,740 Wh (84%) out of the Jackery Explorer 2000 v2. No named reviewer has published a measurement for the 4Patriots 2200X.
standout_why: I opened these rival pages: powerstationgearlab.com ('we don't test products ourselves', so no measured figure for any model), solar-home.space ('Solar Home does not test products', and it estimates runtime with an assumed 0.85 factor), powerstations.reviews/4patriots-solar-generator (runtime = rated × 0.85 ÷ watts, no named test) and theoutagebrief.com ('We have not hands-on tested any of these units'). All seven ChatGPT answers also used an assumed 85% usable-energy figure, never a measured one. I could not open solargenadvisor.com or unpluggedwatts.com (certificate error), popularmechanics.com (fetch blocked) or Consumer Reports (paywall), so I can't rule out that those pages carry measured figures. Popular Mechanics and Consumer Reports appeared in only one of the seven chats.
decides: This supports keeping the BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 as the lead alternative. StorageReview measured it delivering 1,910 Wh, the highest usable AC energy of any candidate with a named test, so the measured 2 kWh class runs from about 1,550 to 1,910 Wh, not a flat 85%. It also gives the page an honest caveat: no reviewer has published a delivered-Wh test of the 4Patriots 2200X. Its 2,240 Wh is the maker's rating, while the rivals' usable numbers are measured. That makes the 4Patriots price per Wh look better than it can be shown to be. The tests used different loads (100 W to 1.8 kW), so present them as separate measurements with the load shown, not as a ranking.

findings.source_title: Portable Power Meets Lab-Grade Reliability: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 Review – StorageReview
findings.note: Lab discharge test with the load between 986 W and 1.1 kW. 'The unit discharged 1.91 kWh.' 1,910 / 2,073.6 Wh rated = 92%.

findings.label: Measured energy to recharge from empty (StorageReview, 2025-04-25)
findings.source_title: Portable Power Meets Lab-Grade Reliability: BLUETTI Elite 200 V2 Review – StorageReview
findings.note: 'For recharging, it required 2.44kWh.' My arithmetic: 1,910 / 2,440 = 78% wall-to-outlet round trip. StorageReview did not publish a percentage.

findings.label: Measured 0–100% AC recharge time (CleanTechnica, 2025-07-07)
findings.source_title: Bluetti Elite 200 V2 Test & Review – CleanTechnica
findings.note: Wall outlet. On two BLUETTI panel arrays the reviewer logged 25% to 100% from 12:00 to 3:39 pm, with 520–550 W initial solar input. The reviewer pushed the load to 3,300 W to overload it, and the unit shut off and needed a reset.

findings.label: Measured usable AC energy (StorageReview, Kevin OBrien, 2023-07-09)
findings.source_title: EcoFlow DELTA 2 Max Portable Power Station Review – StorageReview
findings.note: 350 W load through the AC inverter. 1,800 / 2,048 Wh = 88%. Recharging took 2,370 Wh at the highest charge rate, so the round trip is 1,800 / 2,370 = 76% (my arithmetic).

findings.label: Measured usable AC energy at about 200 W (Notebookcheck, Marcus Schwarten, published 2026-02-24, updated 2026-10-05)
findings.source_title: 11.6 kg lighter than its predecessor: Powerstation Anker Solix C2000 Gen 2 review – Notebookcheck
findings.note: Notebookcheck calls 79% 'not a good value'. At an 1,800 W AC load it measured about 1,850 Wh (about 90%). An AC recharge drew almost 2,350 Wh from the wall. It measured about 35 dB at 1 m under high load.

findings.note: The spec table on the same page says 1,710 Wh and 84%. No test load in watts is stated. Measured AC charge: 0–100% in 2.5 h at 817 Wh/h.

findings.source_title: AllPowers R2500 V2: Recensione Power Station 1920Wh – Your Life Updated

unsourced: 4Patriots Patriot Power Generator 2200X measured usable capacity, efficiency or recharge time. I searched for a named lab or reviewer test. GearDiary's 2026-01-20 hands-on review returned HTTP 403. Consumer Reports has a lab page only for the older Patriot Power 1800, behind a paywall. Every other 2200X page I found repeats the 2,240 Wh rating or applies an assumed 85%.

BLUETTI AC180 measured usable capacity: not researched within the tool budget.
Popular Mechanics (2026-11-06) measured figures for the Elite 200 V2 and others: the fetch was blocked, so its test numbers are unverified.
